en: Wept consumed by their own grief.
When a hero leaves a widowed wife,
This vain world lies desolate;
When a son remains without seeing his father,
When the river dries and leaves only its bed,
When darkness covers human eyes—
“This is calamity,” they cried.
The multitude wailed in an uproar;
Black Giant and Kyzylsart mourned
As though the leopard-like hero had died that very day.
It was as though they had dug the earth with mattocks,
Recited his funeral prayer with due honour,
And buried him with the congregation that day;
As though they had laid him in his coffin,
The nation groaned and the people clamoured,
As though carrying him to the grave.
Black Giant and Kyzylsart
Grieved, the two khans weeping;
The khan and all the people wept,
Their hearts deeply stirred
For the woman Aichürök,
As countless hardships loomed ahead.
Her black hair untouched by a comb—
Aichürök wept until she was spent
And spread it strand by strand;
Her precious hair, long as meadow grass,
She spread across her breast.
Your kinsman Kyzylsart—
When she saw Kyzylsart,
It seemed her precious sultan had died.
The people cried out and the nation stirred,
As though burying their great warrior that day.
She raised a piercing cry,
And her white face, lovely as a plane tree—
Alas for the frailty of woman—
She clawed and tore again and again.
Dark blood flowed where she tore,
And Aichürök’s strength departed;
Her pale complexion faded,
And the blood flowing from both cheeks
Poured down over her breast.
Blood streamed like water through a ditch,
And Aichürök’s strength departed.
Hear how she raised her wailing voice,
Lamenting for her vanished lord:
“A charger that would not tire in six months’ riding
You were, my princely khan.
A falcon that took the wolf when properly flown
You were, my princely khan.
If ten thousand rivers joined,
You were their confluence, my princely khan.
If ten thousand cliffs joined,
You were their mighty collision, my princely khan.
Of the heavens and the blue sky
You were the supporting pillar, my princely khan.
Among ravenous lion-warriors
You alone were supreme, my princely khan.
Those upon whom you fixed your gaze
You would subdue, my princely khan.
Those who faced you eye to eye you conquered—
A star stirred in the heavens,
And in one night she awoke a thousand times;
She nursed me on her pure white milk
And fed me grains of white wheat.
She had an amulet hung around my neck,
Lest the enemy’s wrath strike me,
And had me raised in tenderness.
She reared me to maturity and made me a hero,
Made me the equal of heroic sons,
And raised a clamour when I was born.
My venerable white-haired mother,
Should the khan’s only prince
Have cause to wander in desolation?
My mother in this dark day, where are our people?
When will the day come that we reach them?
Should a noble prince’s only son
Have cause to roam as an exile?
My ill-fated mother, where are our people?
Across the yellow, rolling uplands,
When will the day come to cross the ridge?
When will we return to the land
Of willow-lined Keng-Kol and broad Talas?
When shall I cross them, dear mother—
Kara-Buura and broad Chatkal?
When shall I see, dear mother,
Those highlands where our people summer?
When shall we return to the uplands,
To my inheritance from my father,
To my Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
To keep court and dwell among the mountains?
When shall we return to the people
Of my ancestral inheritance,
Who play orompoi and strike the ordo stones?
When shall we cross the ridges
Of the two passes, Küyük and Chakmak?
When shall the mighty Kyrgyz and the many Argyn
Camp together in their villages
And open their hearts to laughter?
When shall we pass through the Seven Valleys
And reach our inheritance?”
The people cried out and the nation wept,
And while the multitude stood thus,
The hero’s son, Er Seytek,
Heard rumours among the people,
And heard that his mother had come.
Then Er Seytek
Heard the tale from Külchoro:
He learned that Semetey, gone to the other world,
Had been his father.
He grew angry and darkened,
His threatening face turned grim;
His black eyes became bloodshot,
His bloodied face turned ashen,
His heart became a fire of burning coals.
If the fierce one turned in wrath,
He became a blazing flame.
He made ready all his weapons,
And the fiery young eagle,
Hung at his side a sword without a sheath.
He heard the voice of the grief-stricken woman Chürök
And was deeply distressed,
Grieving for the lion father
Who had vanished from sight.
Seytek trembled violently,
His two cheeks turning pale;
The peerless grey-maned hero’s
Old wound of sorrow opened anew.
His gleaming teeth clenched together;
When the hero grew angry,
He seemed a fortress raised upon the hills,
And when he merely stirred,
He seemed ready to devour all mankind.
Leaning upon his keen blade,
His long, bony knees bending,
Er Seytek came running
To his mother:
“My dearest mother,
My gentle mother who cradled me,
Until the five Arkar stars had set,
You nursed me five times through the night,
Lashed by the whip, my flesh was torn,
My blood poured darkly forth.
They made me settle all accounts,
And slashed my breasts to wounds.
They stripped me of all my possessions,
My splendid gown and flowing trousers—
Your wretched mother has endured countless sorrows.
They had my fine clothes torn to shreds,
An arrow struck me in the horde, and I was captured;
Thinking back, I was beaten soft as wool,
Endured great misery and was sold,
And this head was bound to torment.
My heart departed, torn asunder,
My poor soul was sorely tried,
And I was dragged like a goat in kökbörü,
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Kept captive, neither dead nor vanished,
Mauled like a goat in kökbörü,
Beaten and made rich plunder.
By day, my daylight turned to night;
Your mother, lovely as the moon,
Was beaten till she became like wool,
And all I saw was a day of darkness.
With death and misery in my thoughts,
You, Seytek, survivor of the ruin,
Poor soul not yet born,
Were six months within my womb.
When your caravan-leading father died,
In my anguish I wished to follow him.
I remained alive, my foal,
For the legacy left by my companion—
The six-month child within my womb,
The poor child, dearest of all.
In Jeti-Özön the Jediger
Dragged me by the nape and made me wool,
Plundered without restraint and made me a slave;
I came to know humiliation and grief,
And my sacred sides
Were lashed and torn by whips,
While my blood poured darkly forth.
Alas, Mother, where are our people?
When shall we reach them?
The Ala-Too, white with snow,
Is our inheritance from our fathers;
When shall we dwell along its skirts?
When shall we tether the many fleet steeds
And barren mares?
When shall we don and proudly toss
Our twin lynx-and-sable caps?
When shall we ride colts and fly falcons,
And live in happiness?
When shall we rally the clamoring people,
Muster an army, and gird our waists?
When shall we pursue the blood-price
Of my lionhearted father, the departed hero?”
Thus spoke the valiant Seytek,
Joining his mother,
And asking her about his people.
Before he had finished asking,
Before he had finished speaking,
Before she could bring herself to tell the dreadful words,
Before she could recount the deeds
Of the vanished blood-stained warrior,
Then Aichürök
Spoke at length of the land:
“Your mighty forefather was the perfect Manas,
And broad Talas was his dwelling place.
That land is your inheritance from your forefather,
Your people, inherited from your father,
Are the legacy that was lost.
My young hero, because of you,
Whatever I grasped became burning embers,
Whatever I crossed became red fire,
Whatever I ate became a bullet of steel.
My hands were bound behind my back;
Helpless under such humiliation,
I yearned for death in earnest.
There was no swift steed to mount,
No kinsman to stand at my side.
The ramparts around me were my very ribs.
When the terrible battle broke out,
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön
There was their seventh, Khan Kyyaz;
When they swept upon us in fury
And reached your princely father,
The moon-crested banner filled the sky,
And a clamor split the heavens.
While battle raged,
The sun grew black and night descended,
And a woeful day of anguish fell.
Though we looked, he was nowhere in sight;
Your leopard father, the blood-stained lion,
No one knew where he was.
However we searched, he could not be seen;
Whether the hero was dead or alive,
No one knew where he was.
His horse failed him and left him on foot,
And the people stripped the clothes from his body.
When the multitude surrounded him, thrusting spears,
And the whole nation came in uproar,
Though we looked, he was nowhere in sight,
And no one knew where he was;
He had mysteriously disappeared.
His dead body was nowhere to be found,
Your blood-stained father had vanished from sight,
And passed into the unseen.
If we follow the lore handed down,
And ask those who know,
They speak confused and rambling words,
And tell many tales that divide the people.
Not one person says, “I saw him”;
We wailed long and grieved,
For thus we lost our gray-maned wolf.
We did not behold the noble hero’s corpse
And bind it with brocade,
Nor wash it with Zamzam water.
